Prevention: Place onion nursery site away from infested crops.
Remove all alternative host plants, such as any wild allium or allium crops near and around the field
Intercrop onions with carrots (Thrips do not like carrots)
Provide good growing conditions for the onions to ensure rapid growth.
Environmental stress weakens plants and makes them more susceptible to thrips attack.
Thrips are not good fliers, but can move with the wind.
Therefore plant younger onions upwind of older plots.
Remove and destroy all the un-harvested crop remains from the field.
Monitoring: Scout for thrips and their damage after formation of onion leaves until one -month before harvesting.
Thrips are very small and thin insect pests (a bit more than 1 mm long).
They are light greyish to greenish or dark greyish, but difficult to see.
Look for groups of thrips and silvery patches caused by many small scratches of thrips feeding on leaf surfaces.
At 10 -20 infested plants observed per ¼ acre of onion field, direct control measures may be considered.
Direct Control: Liquid soap spray (stir 3 tablespoons liquid soap, e.g.
Cera-liquid, with 4 litres water) is effective during moist conditions, and when sprayed at least 2 x in a week interval.
Grind 1 kg of fresh leaves of neem or ripened seeds and in 10 litres of water overnight.
Sieve the mixture, add 1 tea spoon of soft soap to 10 litres of solution.
Stir and spray once every two weeks.
Grind one handful of hot pepper and soak in 10 litres of water overnight; then sieve.
To avoid phototoxic effects of sprays on the plants, do not spray in full sun or during dry periods.
Sprays should cover the entire plant surface until it reaches the lower part of the onion where thrips eat.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
